Almost as much as you will give us.
I will take the answer given by the hon." member (Mr. Power).
Unfortunately I am not in a position to give very definite information, but I may say that the facilities at present can take care of ten times the traffic we now have.

That is the point I wish to make; we have already at the port of Quebec facilities for handling a great many more cattle without further expenditures. I have listened to this debate both to-night and the other evening, and I have been siienlt, but I intend to vote against these proposals, and not because I am antagonistic to Quebec, as I have repeatedly said from this corner of the House; I think we have all proved at least that we have a warm feeling for the port of Quebec. We feel that Montreal has hogged the puck to the detriment of the port of Quebec and also to the detriment of eastern ports of the Maritime provinces. We would like to see the port of Quebec developed, and to see more business go through it. I find that in 1924 there were transported1 through the port of Quebec exactly 1,507 head of cattle, and that at the same time 44,494 went through the port of Montreal. When the government propose to spend $5,000,000 to build facilities at the port of Quebec they should show us that .more business can be done there. We are sympathetic to the port of Quebec. We have the Transcontinental railway and we would like to patronize it; we are capable of shipping the cattle and of furnishing the wheat. We also have the elevator space. Last year five million bushels were handled at the Quebec elevator and grain men tell me that the facilities there are capable af handling three, four or five times as many bushels of grain-someone suggests forty million bushels. So why in the name of economy should we Spend $5,000,000 to extend facilities at the port of Quebec, which, I understand,-and someone will correct me if I am wrong-are not used' to their full capacity at present? I protest against this expenditure, and if it comes to a vote I will vote against it.

The minister did not answer my last question, as to how much the government can still advance to the harbour commissioners of Quebec apart from this legislation. I wonder if he would also give us some indication as to how much of this proposed loan or guaranteed1 loan the commissioners intend to spend during the coming year. If we could get this information we might have an intelligent grasp of just what is at stake.

The amount of money
which can be advanced to the Quebec Harbour Commissioners under existing legislation is about $100,000. As to my hon. friend's second question, the harbour commissioners will not be in a position to spend more than $1,000,000 during the first year.
Mr. Chairman-
Carried.

Hon. gentleman are in too much of a hurry. Notwithstanding all that has been said, I am still unconvinced that this large grant to the port of Quebec harbour is needed. It has not been shown that the present capacity is used to its full extent. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) need not say that bitterness is shown on this side of the House as against Quebec, because since the Progressive party have come here in considerable numbers we have pleaded for the port of Quebec. I have in mind speeches made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) and also the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) on behalf of the port of Quebec, asking that it get its share. But what has been the influence that has kept Quebec from getting its full share of traffic in the years gone by? Can any gentleman on that side say that that influence has been removed and that Quebec is going to get its full share after this? Notwithstanding the fact that, according to the minister himself, over $21,000,000 have been invested1 in the port of Quebec by the Dominion, on which is owing some $8,077,000, we are asked to vote an additional $5,000,000 for a harbour that is not at present used to its full capacity. It has been said that the largest boats that go up the St. Lawrence cannot dock there, but I know for a fact that the Regina docks there without any trouble.

Will the hon. gentleman
pardon me if I simply add that in 1923 the Regina was unable to take a full cargo at Montreal and had to take a full cargo at Quebec? I have a long list of vessels which in the summer of 1923 were in the same posi-

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
tion, and I am willing to read! them to my hon. friend.
What tonnage of general cargo passed through the port of Quebec last year?
It was 594,000 tons.

Can the minister give
any information as to the source of that tonnage?

It was grain, coal, fuel oil
and general cargo.

What was the tonnage
of coal and grain respectively?

Coal, 246,227 tons; grain,
157,975 tons; general cargo, 100,000 tons. This does not include lumber and timber.

Can the minister say
where this general cargo originated?
I am afraid not.

Was the general cargo
both out and in?
Yes.

I would like to say a
word by way of protest against this vote. As far as I can see there seems to be very little possibility of the port of Quebec developing unitil such time as we get a freight rate to that port that will draw traffic there. I know for a fact- that when the grain passes out of the hands of the farmers of western Canada, and that is when it reaches Fort Wfilliam, they have nothing at al' to say about its destination. This House may be well assured that those who are shipping grain to Great Britain and other European ports will ship their grain by the cheapest route. We have heard, for instance, that the Saskatchewan Elevator Company have recently built a large elevator at Buffalo. They have built it there simply because it is the probable route over which most of the grain will go, to the detriment of the Georgian bay ports. It seems to me that if this government or any other government that may come into existence in the future desires to make the Canadian ports what they should be, they will first of all have to take into consideration how best to get the traffic that should pass through our ports to those ports at the lowest possible cost. I believe the prime duty of the government at the present time is an adjustment of railway rates, for instance, to the port of Quebec, and until the government take hold of this question in such a way that they will bring results, I for one am opposed to the expending of more money on this post. When the government can show us that they are in earnest, that they will see to it that the tonnage that goes out of Canada and the tonnage that comes into Canada is going to be carried through our own ports at rates equal to what it can be carried to other ports in the United States, I shall be quite willing to support the government in any expenditure to make our Canadian ports what they should be.

The figures of 1,507 head of cattle were given as the number exported from the port of Quebec. It seems to me that the farmers of Quebec themselves must be very negligent in that they have failed to raise more steers for export from their own ports, if they think this expenditure is necessary.

They are more engaged in dairying than in the raising of cattle.

Quebec Harbour Commissioners

I have to admire the generosity of this government in providing further facilities for the port of Quebec for the benefit of the himterland west of the Great Lakes, whose representatives are opposed to this expenditure. If the people of Quebec really require the development of their port, surely they would have been creating more traffic for it; but judging from that standpoint, they apparently do not want this development.
It has been stated here to-night that for good business reasons western grain cannot go to the port of Quebec simply because to provide the necessary rolling stock to carry it there would plunge the road almost irretrievably into debt, irrespective of what the rates might be. I have information by letter from the west from farmers living along the international boundary that there is a considerable sentiment backwards and forwards between the farmers out there in favour of reciprocity with Canada. We in Canada have on our statute books at the present time an offer of reciprocity to the United States. I might also state that in the morning press I saw the view expressed that the day was not far distant when the United States would again approach Canada with the object 12 m. of bringing about reciprocity or an exchange of natural products. When that day comes the Fordney-McCumiber tariff of 40 cents a bushel on wheat is going to be taken off. I believe the United States government now realize the folly of that imposition on our export wheat, and also on our cattle. That in itself is going to militate against the business that might otherwise go to Quebec harbour and our far eastern ports.
Does the hon. member want to persuade us to vote against reciprocity?

I do not think it is possible to make a speech that would persuade the hon. member to vote against reciprocity. I have never voted against it myself. I have always supported that principle, and I would vote for it to-night or at any other time when the opportunity was presented.
But if my hon. friend shows us that it would be better for us not to support reciprocity, we shall find1 it extremely difficult to persuade our people at home that they should support it.

I am trying to show what
would result from a freer interchange of trade between the two countries. It might benefit us all. I believe that there are scores of members on the government side of the House who are opposed from a business point of view to spending $5,000,000 in Quebec harbour.
Look on your own side.

I quite anticipate what the
vote will be, but let us be frank and admit that votes are not always given on the merits of the question.
Oh, yes, on this side.

I am going to refer for a
moment to the remarks made by the Minister of Justice. Surely he does not charge the members in this corner of the House with being antagonistic to the people of Quebec or to Quebec harbour. I would not like to have that inference drawn because I am taking the stand I do simply from a business standpoint. I do not think any evidence has been adduced up to the present time which warrants this huge expenditure. Almost one might be tempted to exclaim, "God save Canada 1" if such things are going to happen, with the government proposing to spend $5,000,000 with our economic conditions are as they are to-day, on a harbour that is not now being used to the utmost of its facilities, and with not much prospect for many years to come of the facilities already available being used to their capacity. This proposal comes from a government that professes economy, that preaches economy from the house-tops. The proposal itself is very good evidence to the contrary, if I am any judge. I shall not have to take the consequences, however; it will not be my funeral. The government must take the responsibility.

Quebec is the
cradle of Canada.

If the government want to
provide these facilities at the port of Quebec, they should provide greater traffic for the port and not depend upon the western provinces to do it. We are not asking for this. We are opposed to the principle, because we do not think that we can supply the Motherland through the port of Quebec and leave any profits to ourselves. I am sure that when the members of the government will look at this question from a purely business point of view, they will realize it is an unwarranted expenditure.

A few minutes ago the minister intimated that further developments at Quebec were endorsed by the president of the Canadian National Railways. I should like to ask him when that endorsement was made, and what was the nature of it. Can he read anything to the House that will convince us that the president of the Canadian National Railways justifies this development or believes it is necessary at the present time?

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
I have not the letter of the president of the Canadian National Railways before me. It was written last year.

What was the nature of the
document?
It was in approval of the proposal that is presently submitted to the House, and which had 'been submitted to him previously by the Quebec harbour commissioners.
Did he intimate in that document that rates would be readjusted to justify us in believing that the volume of grain moving to Quebec would be greater in the future?

He did not refer to rates
in the letter.

I am not going to make
any speech on this question, but I am going to vote for this loan. I think that with the exception of the members from Quebec themselves I know more about the Quebec harbour development than any man in this House. I was identified with it many years ago, and we provided for a great development along . these waters-that was the original plan- from Cap Rouge down to the city of Quebec. Proper: y was purchased at that time to carry out harbour development right along the front where there was deep water. That was changed, but I am not going to discuss it at the present time. I want to ask my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) a question. He surprised me if I got the thing right. He mentioned some company or some organization that was building an elevator at Buffalo. Now, will my hon. friend repeat the name of that organization?
The Saskatchewan Cooperative Elevator Company Lihiited.

That is sending Canadian
trade through Canadian ports.
That is all I want to know.

The Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company Limited seems to be a rather interesting subject just now. I have been connected with that company. I happen to have been a director on the board for nine years, and I was on the board when the decision to build that elevator was arrived at. The Minister of Railways and Canals seems rather surprised. He would be more surprised if I said the action of this government had a very large influence in determining the building of that elevator at Buffalo. I can assure, him, that it had.
In what way?

I will explain to the Minister of Railways in what way. We discussed the question of lake freight rates at very great length in this House. It was pointed out that grain was carried by Canadian beats to Buffalo, a three day journey, at less money than it was carried to Georgian Bay ports which is a two day journey. I adked the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, not the present minister, if when there was half a cent a bushel discrimination in favour of Buffalo' he would say that the coasting laws should be automa: ically suspended!? His answer was "Why should I?" I went from here to Regina to a meeting of the Saskatche-man Co-operative Elevator board. We were rather in favour cf building at a Georgian bay port and had been considering it. The question of Buffalo came up. My1 mind was made up from the moment I got the minister's answer. Not only did we have the advantage of a lower rate to Buffalo carrying our grain farther on its way, but I want to say that Buffalo is the most advantageous point on this continent for grain to be at. It can be shipped from there to Montreal; it can be shipped to New York, to Philadelphia, to Boston, to many of these ports that are open all the year round. I tell this House that this business of carrying grain to Quebec is a myth. Not only is there a long railway haul, but the farmers are unable to collect from the railway company any of the shortages which are incurred by reason of that long haul. So what do they do? They get their wheat into a place where they can get their weight as quickly as possible; that is Fort William. As has been pointed out, the wheat has left the farmer's hands at this time and is in the hands of the exporters. When you go to talk business with these men you have to talk business. As we have been told, grain is like water; it will run down hill, and all the talk, and all the sentiment, and all the patriotism will not make it run up hill. Grain will follow the line of least resistance in spite of all preaching to the contrary. Some hon. members say "patriotism". Is my company any more unpatriotic than the lake shipping companies? Are we any more unpatriotic than a member of this government who will not put into effect the suspension of the coasting laws? Let me point out one other reason why grain will never go to Quebec which my hon. friends apparently do not know. When navigation is closing it is the practice at the head of the lakes to load every available boat for winter storage, which can be got on these boats at about half the price that it can be got for in elevators. Every available boat that can be

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
loaded is sent down to Buffalo for the last journey. There is an ice breaker in Buffalo harbour, and the boats can be moved to the transfer houses and unloaded, the grain loaded in cars, and in twenty-four hours shipped to New York.
Will my hon. friend tell me the total amount of grain which is stored in these bottoms?

I have not the figures here but I can assure my hon. friend it is a considerable quantity.
'Mr. VIEN: Is it not a fact that it is a trifling amount as compared with the volume that is being transported?
The quantity is more than the port of Quebec handles altogether.

That is why we want
facilities for handling more.

No man owning an elevator that was only filled to twice its capacity would ever dream of enlarging the capacity of that elevator. In the case of the Buffalo elevator we will consider that if it is not filled ten times in the course of the year it will be doing poor business.
My hon. friend was speaking of winter storage. He cannot avail himself of the advantage more than once in the winter. Once the boats are loaded and jammed in ice they do not reload them.

That is only one advantage which is possessed at Buffalo and nowhere else. The ice is not so thick but that the ice breakers can keep the harbour open. These boats can be moved up in the winter time and unloaded and the grain delivered to ports that are open all the year.

At any time in the
winter?

At any time in the winter. There is this further advantage in favour of grain at the head of the lakes. Quebec has only one market, and that is the market overseas. At the head of the lakes grain can go by three or four different routes.
I am not going to speak at much greater length. I spoke on this question a few nights ago when I said I could not support this vote. Like the Minister of Railways I am going to vote, and I shall vote against the proposition if a vote is called. My reasons for taking that stand are these:	All these
things would be very nice if we could afford them, if we had the money. In conducting my own business if I cannot afford a thing

I have to go without it. It is time this government adopted the same method. On our political platforms we preach economy to the country. We also preach it in this House; and economy will be advocated when we go to the country on every political platform. But the question I want to know is when are we going to begin to practise economy. A few nights ago it was stated that we could not afford to reconsider the question of revaluing soldier settlement lands. We could not afford it. One hon. gentleman opposite also made the statement that we on this side were asking for everything. I want to tell 'the House that I represent one of the oldest constituencies in the west. We have been paying taxes all these years and we have not got a brick or a stick or anything in the shape of a government building, in the whole of that constituency. I should like to know what my people would say to me on my return home if I voted for this $5,000,000, when no valid reason has been given for the vote. I cannot do it. The Minister of |Judtice accused Ime of being rather unfair. I have looked at my words, and I am going to give him credit for think-, ing that he does not want to be unfair to me. I said:
We were told that there had not been a ship in that drydock. If my information was wrong, I cannot help it.
Mr. Lapointe: What time of the year was that?
Mr. Sales: I believe in June-May.
Mr. Lapointe: I think it was in May.
Mr. Sales: Perhaps it was. But that was the information we received, and we did not know any better. If it was wrong, I am glad to be corrected.

speechtext:
My friend said he saw
dust. He was not told there was dust; he saw it.
I did.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There is always dust in
those shops.

I did not need to put my
spectacles on to see it either. The dust was in the workshop. The private dock was being used. The government dock was empty. But I do not want to discuss that point any further. I think I have proved to my hon. friend that I did not want to be unfair, and that I did not say anything that was unfair.
Will not my hon. friend admit that a dry-dock is like a hospital?-when it is not being used it is because shipping is in a healthy condition.

That is just like saying they
do not need any dredging.

Quebec Harbour Commissioners

My hon. friend's imagination,
of course, is very fertile. I expect there is not enough business in Quebec for the shipping to get out of order; therefore the dust probably would accumulate. But we will let that matter pass.

But my hon. friend will not
contend that the St. Lawrence route should not be equipped with a dry-dock capable of receiving the largest steamers that ply in those waters?

Not at all. Let me say this, Mr. Chairman, and I am through: the moment Quebec can show me that her facilities are being used to their capacity, or anywhere near their capacity, I will be the first man in this House to vote for the development of the port.

Mr. Chairman, the minister took exception to the figures I submitted earlier in the debate when I stated that 1,507 head of cattle went through the port of Quebec last year. I received the figures from the Live Stock Commissioner and I have no doubt they are authentic. I sent them over to the minister, and he was kind enough to give me the figures for 1923-5,046. Now, I submit in all seriousness that the members who are agitating for this vote had better try and secure the lost tonnage that should have gone through the port last year. Remember, 5,046 cattle went through the port in 1923 and only 1,507 in 1924, and yet those members ask for an additional $5,000,000 to develop the facilities at that port.
May I tell my hon. friend that already 1,500 head of cattle have gone through the port this season, so we are following his advice.
I am glad to hear that.

Not at all, Mr. Chairman. One of the members for Quebec stated a few moments ago that the present facilities at Quebec are capable of handling all the cattlp we can send them.
For the time being.

As a cattle man engaged in the business, I hope to see the day when
40,000	or 50,000 head will be rolling through the port of Quebec.
